pedagogy.summary: Children learn that a line of symmetry is a fold line: a line about which one half of a figure maps exactly onto the other. They find ALL such lines in a shape, recognise shapes that have none, and — crucially — do this whatever the shape's orientation. The defining idea is the fold-and-match test, not a counting rule: a rectangle has two lines of symmetry (through the midpoints of opposite sides), not four, and its diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry because folding along a diagonal leaves the halves misaligned. Symmetry is a structural property to be tested, never read off the number of sides.
bestPractices: Define a line of symmetry operationally — fold along it and the two halves must coincide exactly; teach children to check by drawing round a shape, cutting it out and folding (mindful that careless cutting distorts the result) (NCETM).

Actively confront the 'lines of symmetry = number of sides' over-generalisation: because early examples are usually regular shapes, children conclude a rectangle has 4 lines — give many NON-regular shapes and have them test each candidate line by folding (NCETM).
Use the rectangle as the anchor counterexample: its 2 real lines (vertical and horizontal through side-midpoints) versus its 2 falsely-assumed diagonals, disproved by folding corner-to-corner.

Present shapes in varied orientations — tilted and rotated, not just upright — so symmetry is judged by structure, not by whether a mirror line happens to be vertical; move the mirror line around (geoboard + elastic band) rather than always drawing it on upright pictures (NCETM).
Teach patterns before shapes — children recognise symmetry in patterns more readily — then progress to naming and drawing lines on shapes (NCETM).
Sort shapes by symmetry (Carroll/Venn: 'no lines', 'exactly one line', 'more than one line') to build precise vocabulary and expose non-symmetric cases.
keyRepresentations: Fold test — physically folding a cut-out shape so halves coincide (the definition made concrete)
Geoboard with an elastic band as a movable mirror line
Mira/mirror placed on a candidate line to see if the reflection completes the shape
Carroll/Venn sorting by number of lines of symmetry
commonMisconceptions: Assuming the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides — so a rectangle is given 4 lines instead of 2 (over-generalised from regular shapes).
Treating a diagonal of a rectangle (or other non-square) as a line of symmetry, when folding along it shows the halves do not match.
Only recognising a line of symmetry when it is vertical/upright, missing symmetry in tilted or rotated shapes.
Thinking every shape must have at least one line of symmetry (not recognising asymmetric shapes).

learn.summary: Children learn that a line of symmetry is a fold line: a line about which one half of a figure maps exactly onto the other. The defining idea is an operational fold-and-match test, not a counting rule. A non-square rectangle has two lines of symmetry (through the midpoints of opposite sides), not four, and its diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry because folding corner-to-corner leaves the halves misaligned (a square, the special rectangle, has 4 lines including its diagonals). Children find ALL lines in a shape, recognise shapes with none, and judge symmetry whatever the shape's orientation. The activities use physical folding of cut-out shapes and movable mirror lines to confront the common 'lines = number of sides' over-generalisation, with item-based and tappable-image formats as complementary assessment and illustration.

activities.title: Fold-and-match test with a drawn candidate line
feedback: When halves coincide exactly, the line is a true line of symmetry; where corners or edges miss, it is not — e.g. an optional green overlay for a match and red where halves fail to meet makes this vivid.
If a learner marks 4 lines on the rectangle, have them fold each: the two diagonals fail, leaving 2 true lines.

If a learner says a diagonal 'cuts it in half so it counts', fold corner-to-corner and look at the corners — 'cuts in half' is not the same as 'folds onto itself'; the two triangles are congruent but do not land on each other under the fold.
If a learner only finds symmetry when a line is upright, keep the shape tilted and fold along the sloping line to show symmetry belongs to the shape, not the page.

A paper or card cut-out has slight thickness and may be imperfectly cut; treat the fold result as testing the ideal flat shape it represents, and re-check a near-miss in case it is only a cutting artefact.
activities.rationale: The misconception lives in the child's own proposed line, so letting them test their OWN candidate lines by folding gives the felt refutation of the counting rule. Physical cut-and-fold, or a model that folds across a drawn line, makes the operational definition concrete; varied orientations prevent the 'symmetry must be upright' habit.
sourceClaims: A key symmetry misconception is that the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides — 'when continually faced with regular shapes, pupils will draw the conclusion that number of lines of symmetry is equal to the number of sides – and nearly always assume 4 lines of symmetry for [a] rectangle'.

Children find recognising symmetry easier with patterns than with shapes (teach in that order); teaching should avoid finding lines of symmetry only on regular polygons and give varied experiences — geoboards with an elastic-band mirror line, completing half a shape, and checking by drawing round, cutting out and folding (mindful careless cutting distorts results).
Year 4 pupils should complete a simple symmetric figure with respect to a specific line of symmetry, and identify lines of symmetry in 2-D shapes presented in different orientations.
learnerActions: Start with a cut-out or on-screen rectangle. Draw where you think each fold line (line of symmetry) should be, and say why before testing.
Fold (or let a screen model fold) one half across each drawn line and check whether the two halves land exactly on top of each other.
Deliberately try a diagonal corner-to-corner: fold along it and watch the far corners — they miss each other, so it is NOT a line of symmetry.
Confirm the vertical and horizontal lines through the side midpoints: these fold to an exact match, so the rectangle has 2 lines, not 4.
Tilt or rotate the shape (e.g. 30-40 degrees) and re-check the same lines are still there without turning the page upright.
Progress to non-regular polygons and a few asymmetric shapes (answer: 0 lines), testing every candidate line by folding.
activities.intendedInsight: A line of symmetry is whatever survives the fold-and-match test, not whatever a count-the-sides rule predicts; symmetry is a structural property of the shape independent of its orientation.

activities.title: Movable mirror line on a geoboard or with a mirror
feedback: If the reflected image does not line up with the existing half, the mirror is not on a line of symmetry — move it and try again.
When completing a half-shape, check the finished figure folds onto itself along the given line.
Careless cutting distorts a cut-out, so a near-miss fold may be a cutting artefact — re-check with a mirror or a cleaner cut-out.
activities.rationale: A movable mirror line decouples symmetry from page orientation and lets children explore many candidate positions; starting from patterns matches the reported ease ordering. Completion tasks rehearse the Year 4 objective of completing a symmetric figure about a specific line.
sourceClaims: Children find recognising symmetry easier with patterns than with shapes (teach in that order); teaching should avoid finding lines of symmetry only on regular polygons and give varied experiences — geoboards with an elastic-band mirror line, completing half a shape, and checking by drawing round, cutting out and folding (mindful careless cutting distorts results).
Year 4 pupils should complete a simple symmetric figure with respect to a specific line of symmetry, and identify lines of symmetry in 2-D shapes presented in different orientations.
learnerActions: Use a geoboard with an elastic band (or a Mira/mirror laid on a candidate line) as a movable mirror line.
Move the mirror line around the shape rather than always drawing it on an upright picture; check whether the reflection completes the shape.
Begin with symmetric patterns before moving to named shapes, recognising symmetry in patterns first.
Complete the missing half of a shape given a specific line of symmetry.
activities.intendedInsight: A mirror line can sit anywhere, and reflection across the right line reproduces the shape; recognising symmetry in patterns builds toward naming and drawing lines on shapes.

activities.title: Sort shapes by number of lines of symmetry
feedback: A shape with no line of symmetry is a valid answer — not every shape is symmetric.

If a learner says the rectangle has 4 lines like the square because both have 4 sides, test the rectangle's diagonals by folding to show it has exactly 2 lines (still in 'more than one line', like the square, but with a different count).
Use the regular hexagon (6 lines, 6 sides), equilateral triangle (3 lines, 3 sides) and rectangle (2 lines, 4 sides) side by side to pin down exactly when the side-count rule works.
When a learner justifies a placement only by counting sides, ask them to fold a candidate line — the regular cases and the rectangle then separate clearly.
activities.rationale: Sorting builds precise vocabulary and brings non-symmetric and non-regular cases into view, which supports attacking the over-generalisation from regular shapes; a sort checks classification but does not itself elicit folding, so each placement is justified by the fold-and-match test. Comparing triangle, square, rectangle and hexagon isolates why the counting rule is only sometimes valid.
sourceClaims: A key symmetry misconception is that the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides — 'when continually faced with regular shapes, pupils will draw the conclusion that number of lines of symmetry is equal to the number of sides – and nearly always assume 4 lines of symmetry for [a] rectangle'.

Children find recognising symmetry easier with patterns than with shapes (teach in that order); teaching should avoid finding lines of symmetry only on regular polygons and give varied experiences — geoboards with an elastic-band mirror line, completing half a shape, and checking by drawing round, cutting out and folding (mindful careless cutting distorts results).
learnerActions: Sort a set of shapes into 'no lines', 'exactly one line', and 'more than one line' using a Carroll or Venn arrangement.
Include non-regular and asymmetric shapes so cases with zero lines appear.
For each shape, justify its placement by the fold-and-match test rather than by counting sides.
Compare an equilateral triangle (3 lines), a square (4 lines), a rectangle (2 lines) and a regular hexagon (6 lines), and discuss when 'lines = sides' holds and when it breaks.
activities.intendedInsight: Symmetry must be tested per shape; 'lines = number of sides' holds only for regular shapes, so the equilateral triangle, square and regular hexagon match their side counts while the (non-regular) rectangle has fewer lines than its 4 sides.

activities.title: Check items and tappable-line illustration (assessment and support)
feedback: For the rectangle item, the answer is 2; choosing 4 signals the count-the-sides rule and choosing the diagonals signals the 'cuts in half' error — both are refuted by folding.

On a tilted shape that does have a line of symmetry, a 'no symmetry' answer usually means the learner is only looking for upright lines; re-test by folding along a sloping line (a tilted asymmetric shape genuinely has 0 lines).
The tappable overlay shows which fixed lines match, but it reveals pre-drawn lines rather than the learner's own guess, so pair it with hands-on folding of a candidate line the learner proposes.
activities.rationale: Items offering 4 and the diagonals as tempting wrong answers help separate the heuristic from the method, because the two give different answers for a rectangle. A tappable fold-reveal illustrates the idea and supports learners, but because it presents fixed lines it does not let the child test their own proposed line, where the misconception actually lives. Recognition items assess the concept but do not themselves generate the fold-and-match evidence the learner must produce.
sourceClaims: A key symmetry misconception is that the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides — 'when continually faced with regular shapes, pupils will draw the conclusion that number of lines of symmetry is equal to the number of sides – and nearly always assume 4 lines of symmetry for [a] rectangle'.
Year 4 pupils should complete a simple symmetric figure with respect to a specific line of symmetry, and identify lines of symmetry in 2-D shapes presented in different orientations.
learnerActions: Answer short items: 'How many lines of symmetry does this rectangle have?' (with 4 and 'the diagonals' as tempting wrong options), draw all lines on a given figure, decide whether a statement about a tilted shape is true or false, and sort shapes by number of lines.
Include at least one tilted shape and one asymmetric shape in any set.
As a lighter support, tap each drawn line on a static shape to reveal a fold overlay showing match or mismatch, and open a flap asking 'does the diagonal work?' answered by the mismatched fold.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and drawing correct lines of symmetry — especially rejecting the rectangle's diagonals and spotting tilted symmetry — demonstrates the fold-and-match concept rather than a counting habit.

constraints: Define a line of symmetry operationally: fold along it and the two halves must coincide exactly. Teach checking by drawing round a shape, cutting it out and folding — but note careless cutting distorts the result, so a near-miss may be a cutting artefact.
Actively confront the 'lines = number of sides' over-generalisation with many NON-regular shapes; do not rely only on regular shapes, which breed the misconception.

Use the rectangle as the anchor counterexample (2 real lines vs 2 falsely assumed diagonals) and contrast with equilateral triangle (3), square (4) and regular hexagon (6) to show the side-count rule holds for regular shapes only.
Present shapes in varied orientations (tilted and rotated), judging symmetry by structure, not by whether a mirror line happens to be vertical.

A paper or card cut-out has slight thickness and can be imperfectly cut; treat it as an approximation of the ideal flat shape whose exact halves coincide, and reason about the mathematical shape it represents rather than the physical card.
Recognition and multiple-choice items assess the concept but do not, by themselves, generate the fold-and-match evidence the learner must produce; pair them with hands-on or learner-proposed folding.

A tappable-line reveal shows fixed, pre-drawn lines; it illustrates the idea but does not let a child test their own candidate line, so use it as support alongside active folding, not as a replacement.
This is planar (line/reflective) symmetry of 2-D shapes; keep away from 3-D planes of symmetry and depth, which are a different topic.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source marks the two NCETM claims as verified:true and the National Curriculum (Year 4) claim as verified:false; this status was not re-checked here, and the Year 4 claim is used only to support orientation/completion items.

The original artefact-fit entries asserted that 'no static picture can deliver' the diagonal refutation and that a conversation 'cannot provide the fold-and-match evidence'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to affordance/limit statements: a static image or dialogue can still teach, but does not let the learner test their own proposed line.

Arithmetic/geometry self-audit: rectangle = 2 lines (vertical and horizontal through side midpoints), square = 4, equilateral triangle = 3, regular hexagon = 6; the diagonals of a non-square rectangle are not lines of symmetry. These are consistent across the source and retained. The '4 lines' and 'diagonals' appear only as labelled tempting wrong options/misconceptions, never as correct answers.
Internal catalog IDs and fit rankings, plus the reteach-prerequisite ID, were removed; the Year-2 vertical-symmetry revisit is retained as an orientation re-test without the ID.

assess.poeTask: Give the child a paper rectangle. Ask them to PREDICT how many lines of symmetry it has and to mark where, saying WHY before folding. Then have them fold along each marked line and OBSERVE which folds make the halves coincide. The prediction of 4 (or of a working diagonal) is violated when the diagonal fold leaves the corners apart — the child then EXPLAINS that only the vertical and horizontal folds match, so there are 2.
probeDeeper: 'You folded along the vertical line and the halves matched. Now fold along a diagonal — what happens to the corners?' (counterexample that refutes the diagonal directly).
'A square has 4 lines of symmetry. Why does this rectangle have fewer, even though both have 4 sides?' (forces reasoning about equal vs unequal sides, not the counting rule).

'A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry — the same as its number of sides. So is "lines = sides" a good rule? When does it work and when does it break?' (tests understanding of WHY the rule holds for regular shapes only).
Rotate the rectangle 40°: 'Does it still have lines of symmetry? Show me where, without turning the page.' (orientation-independence).
assess.correctAnswer: Two lines of symmetry — one vertical and one horizontal, each through the midpoints of opposite sides. The child justifies each by the fold-and-match test (folding along the line, the two halves land exactly on each other) and explains that the diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry because folding corner-to-corner leaves the halves misaligned.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides, so a rectangle 'has 4' ('four sides, four lines')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold the rectangle along each proposed line; the diagonals fail. Contrast with the square (4) and a regular hexagon (6) to show the rule holds ONLY for regular shapes, and have the child test many non-regular shapes.
errorPatterns.distractor: 4 lines of symmetry — one for each side
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States 4 lines for the rectangle; applies a counting rule rather than folding; often confident because it worked on squares and regular shapes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a diagonal of the rectangle as a line of symmetry (fold corner-to-corner)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold along the diagonal and look at the corners — they do not meet; the two triangles are congruent but reflected the wrong way. Establish that 'cuts it in half' is not the same as 'folds onto itself'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The two diagonals are also lines of symmetry
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws one or both diagonals as lines of symmetry and claims the halves 'match'; has not actually tested the fold, or judges by the line 'splitting it in two' rather than by congruent reflection.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only recognises a line of symmetry when it is vertical/upright, missing symmetry in a tilted or rotated shape
errorPatterns.nextMove: Keep the shape tilted and use a mirror/fold along a sloping line; show symmetry is a property of the shape, not of the page orientation. Revisit vertical-only symmetry from Year 2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a rotated shape (surfaced by a follow-up), finds no line or only a would-be vertical one; needs to turn the shape upright before spotting symmetry.

responseLevels.gap: Counts lines of symmetry as the number of sides (rectangle = 4), includes diagonals, and/or only looks for a vertical line; cannot justify by folding.
responseLevels.full: Identifies all and only the true lines of symmetry by the fold-onto-itself test, rejects the rectangle's diagonals with a corner-mismatch justification, finds symmetry regardless of orientation, and explains that 'lines = sides' holds for regular shapes only — transferring correctly to non-regular and asymmetric shapes.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the two true lines by folding on an upright shape but cannot fully justify why the diagonals fail, or reverts to the counting rule on an unfamiliar shape, or misses symmetry when the shape is tilted. Can list lines but not explain the fold-and-match criterion or transfer it to rotated/non-regular cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show an upright rectangle (clearly not a square). Ask: 'How many lines of symmetry does this rectangle have? Draw each one. Then tell me: how do you KNOW each line you drew is a line of symmetry — and how would you decide whether a line is NOT one?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The rectangle is the decisive shape: a child using the 'lines = number of sides' rule answers 4 (adding the two diagonals), while a child using the fold-and-match test answers 2 — the heuristic and the correct method give DIFFERENT answers here, so the response separates them. The reason tier is essential: some children draw 2 lines by imitation but cannot say why the diagonals fail, revealing a fragile concept.
